topic.title: Expanding three linear brackets
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: FM1 is a single 2-hour calculator paper of 100 marks with 13 to 15 questions. A three-bracket expansion appears in most series and is nearly always worth 3 marks: Summer 2019 Q12(i) and Summer 2026 Q5 print it on its own, and Summer 2023 Q12(iii) and Summer 2022 Q9(a) place it inside a longer question as the step that feeds a differentiation or a subtraction. Schemes run MW1 for the first pair, MW1 for the multiplication by the third bracket and MW1 for the collected answer; when it sits inside a bigger question the later parts follow through from it.
mustMemorise: Expand two of the brackets first, then multiply that quadratic by the remaining bracket
Three terms times two terms is six products; count them before collecting
The coefficient of x³ is the product of the three x coefficients
The constant term is the product of the three constants
A product that is being subtracted goes inside brackets, and every sign inside changes
Write the answer in descending powers of x
notOnThisSpec: The binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle for (a + b)ⁿ — neither is named anywhere in the Further Mathematics specification or the Teacher Guidance; FM1-ALM-01 asks only for three linear brackets
The factor theorem and the remainder theorem, so you are never asked to factorise a cubic back into three brackets
Brackets containing a squared or fractional term, such as (x² + 1)(x − 3)(x + 2); the statement says three linear brackets
Partial fractions, which belong to A level and do not appear in this specification

mustBeAbleTo: Expand two linear brackets and collect the result into a quadratic
Multiply a three-term quadratic by a linear bracket, producing all six products
Collect like terms and present a cubic in descending powers of x
Handle a bracket printed the other way round, such as (3 − x), without reversing it
Expand a squared bracket times a third bracket by writing the square out as two brackets
Check an expansion using the product of the three x coefficients and the product of the three constants
Subtract one expanded expression from another by bracketing the subtracted one and changing every sign
Substitute a value of x into either the bracket form or the expanded form and get the same number
sheet.howExamined: FM1 is a single 2-hour calculator paper of 100 marks with 13 to 15 questions. A three-bracket expansion appears in most series and is nearly always worth 3 marks: Summer 2019 Q12(i) and Summer 2026 Q5 print it on its own, and Summer 2023 Q12(iii) and Summer 2022 Q9(a) place it inside a longer question as the step that feeds a differentiation or a subtraction. Schemes run MW1 for the first pair, MW1 for the multiplication by the third bracket and MW1 for the collected answer; when it sits inside a bigger question the later parts follow through from it.
traps: Multiplying the quadratic by only part of the third bracket, so three products are missing (Summer 2023 Q12(iii), where the reported errors came from not using brackets around terms)
Subtracting an expanded expression without bracketing it, so only the first term changes sign (Summer 2022 Q9(a), where this cost the final mark for many candidates)
Dividing a correct expansion by a common factor and offering that as the answer, which is a different expression (Summer 2022 Q9(a))
Reversing a bracket such as (3 − x) into (x − 3), which flips the sign of every term of the expansion
Leaving the six products uncollected on the answer line, when the last mark is for the collected cubic
Treating a squared bracket as a single bracket instead of writing it out twice

Expanding correctly and then losing the marks in the gathering: when your expansion is substituted into a larger expression, collect one power at a time rather than in a single sweep (Summer 2019 Q12(ii))

noteBlocks.lede: Three brackets multiplied together is two brackets multiplied together, twice. Expand any pair, collect, then multiply the quadratic you are left with by the bracket still waiting. Six products come out of that second step, and counting them is how you know none has gone missing.
can: Expand a pair of brackets, then multiply that quadratic by the third.
Count six products, and collect them in descending powers.
Write both ends first, keep a reversed bracket, bracket a subtraction.

noteBlocks.md: A product of three things can be grouped any way you like: $abc$ is $(ab)c$. So expand any two brackets and collect, which leaves a quadratic times one bracket. Then multiply every term of the quadratic by every term of that bracket, and collect again in descending powers. Which pair you start with makes no difference to the answer, so pick the simplest.

steps.decision: Any pair will do; expand it and collect first.
The x of the third bracket meets all three terms.
Then the −1 meets all three: six products in all.
Collect like terms, highest power first.

noteBlocks.explain: Expand a pair, then multiply by the third, as steps 1 to 3 of See it did: $(x + 2)(x - 3) = x^{2} - x - 6$, and the $x$ and the $4$ of $(x + 4)$ each meet all three terms. $x^{3} - x^{2} - 6x$ used only the $x$; $x^{3} - 24$ kept only the two ends.

twin.explain: $(x - 1)(x + 4) = x^{2} + 3x - 4$; its three terms meet the $x$ and the $2$ of $(x + 2)$: six products, collected. $x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 4x$ used only the $x$; $x^{3} - 8$ kept only the ends.

optionNotes.why: Only the x of the last bracket was used.
Only the two ends were kept.
The quadratic met only the x of the last bracket; the 4 has to meet all three terms as well.
Only the two ends were kept; the middle products are missing.

noteBlocks.md: You can write down both ends of the answer before expanding anything. The $x^{3}$ term needs an $x$ from every bracket, so it is the three $x$ terms multiplied. The constant needs a number from every bracket, so it is the three numbers multiplied. If your answer disagrees at either end, a product is missing.

noteBlocks.title: Why nothing else reaches either end
noteBlocks.md: Every other product takes an $x$ from some brackets and a number from the rest, so its power lies strictly between: $x^{2}$ or $x$. Only the all-$x$ product makes $x^{3}$, and only the all-number product makes the constant.

noteBlocks.caption: The two ends of $(3x + 2)(x - 5)(2x - 1)$, written before any expanding.

noteBlocks.stem: Write down the $x^{3}$ term and the constant term of $(3x + 2)(x - 5)(2x - 1)$ without expanding.

steps.decision: An x from every bracket: the only way to reach x³.
A number from every bracket: two negatives make the constant positive.
The middle terms need the full expansion; the two ends are the check on it.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the constant term in the expansion of $(x - 1)(x - 6)(x + 4)$?
noteBlocks.explain: The constant is the three numbers multiplied, as step 2 of See it did: $(-1) \times (-6) \times 4 = 24$. Two negative numbers leave it positive; an odd number of them would leave it negative.

twin.prompt: What is the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the expansion of $(3x + 1)(2x - 5)(x + 7)$?
twin.explain: The $x^{3}$ term is the three $x$ terms multiplied: $3x \times 2x \times x = 6x^{3}$, so the coefficient is 6.

noteBlocks.md: Every term of the quadratic meets every term of the last bracket, so before collecting count the products: the terms in one times the terms in the other. The commonest lost mark is a product that never gets written: the quadratic is multiplied by the $x$ term of the last bracket and the number is forgotten. Write one row for each term of the last bracket, count, then collect.

steps.decision: The two simpler brackets first.
The 3x meets all three terms: three products.
The +1 meets them too: three more, six in all.
Collect: −12x² + x² and −36x − 4x. Check the ends: 3x³ and −12.

noteBlocks.title: Expanding Three Brackets
noteBlocks.why: The two-at-a-time routine written out at the speed of a hand, beside our own steps above.

noteBlocks.prompt: Multiplying $x^{2} - 9$ by $2x + 5$, how many products do you write before collecting?
noteBlocks.explain: Count terms times terms, as steps 2 and 3 of See it wrote one row for each term of the last bracket. Here $x^{2} - 9$ has only two terms, so each row holds two products: $2 \times 2 = 4$. Six needs a three-term quadratic; two is one row only.

twin.prompt: Multiplying $x^{2} + 2x - 8$ by $3x - 1$, how many products do you write before collecting?
twin.explain: Three terms meet two terms: $3 \times 2 = 6$, a row of three for the $3x$ and a row of three for the $-1$.

optionNotes.why: Four fits a two-term quadratic; $x^{2} + 2x - 8$ has three terms.
Three is one row only: the $-1$ must meet all three terms as well.
Six fits a three-term quadratic; $x^{2} - 9$ has only two terms, so each row holds two.
Two is one row only: the $5$ must meet both terms as well.

noteBlocks.text: A bracket written the other way round

noteBlocks.md: Papers sometimes print a bracket with the number first, such as $(4 - x)$. Keep it exactly as printed: turning it into $(x - 4)$ changes the expression and flips the sign of every term of the answer. The $x^{3}$ term then comes out negative, which is the quick check.

steps.decision: As printed: 4x + 4 − x² − x.
The x meets all three terms.
The −3 meets them too; a minus times a minus is a plus.
Collect. The ends check: (−1)(1)(1) gives −x³, and 4 × 1 × (−3) gives −12.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which is $(5 - x)(x + 2)(x - 1)$ expanded and simplified?
noteBlocks.explain: Keep $(5 - x)$ as printed, as step 1 of See it kept $(4 - x)$: $(5 - x)(x + 2) = -x^{2} + 3x + 10$, then its three terms meet the $x$ and the $-1$. $x^{3} - 4x^{2} - 7x + 10$ turned the bracket round; $-x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 10x$ used only the $x$.

twin.prompt: Which is $(2 - x)(x + 5)(x + 1)$ expanded and simplified?
twin.explain: As printed, $(2 - x)(x + 5) = -x^{2} - 3x + 10$; its terms meet the $x$ and the $1$. The positive $x^{3}$ answer turned the bracket round; $-x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 10x$ dropped the $1$.

optionNotes.why: The bracket was turned round, flipping every sign.
The 1 of the last bracket was dropped.
The bracket was turned round to (x − 5), which flips every sign of the answer.
Only the x of the last bracket was used; the −1 must meet all three terms.

noteBlocks.md: Sometimes a second expansion is taken away from the first. Write what is being subtracted inside a bracket with the minus in front, then remove the bracket on the next line, changing the sign of every term inside it.

noteBlocks.title: What Summer 2022 found
noteBlocks.md: Summer 2022 Q9(a): most expanded both expressions correctly, then many lost the final mark by not subtracting every term of the quadratic; the report asked for brackets. Some reached the right answer and divided it by 2, which gives a different expression.

noteBlocks.caption: Kept in a bracket, the minus reaches every term: all three signs change.

steps.decision: Choosing the easy pair first: a difference of two squares.
A squared bracket is the bracket written twice.
What is subtracted goes in a bracket, minus sign in front.
Every sign in the bracket changes, then collect.

noteBlocks.prompt: You have expanded a cubic and now have to subtract a quadratic from it. What do you write first?
options: The quadratic inside brackets, with the minus sign in front of the bracket
The quadratic with its first term's sign changed
The two expressions side by side and collect straight away
noteBlocks.answer: The quadratic inside brackets, with the minus sign in front of the bracket
noteBlocks.explain: The bracket is what lets the minus reach every term, as step 3 of See it wrote it before step 4 changed all three signs. Changing only the first sign, or collecting straight away, loses the other terms' signs, which is how the Summer 2022 final mark went.

twin.prompt: From an expanded cubic you must subtract $(2x - 1)^{2}$. Which line comes next?
twin.explain: $(2x - 1)^{2} = 4x^{2} - 4x + 1$, and all of it is subtracted: bracket it, then every sign changes to $-4x^{2} + 4x - 1$. Changing one sign, or none, leaves terms added that should be taken away.

optionNotes.why: Only the first sign changed; the minus reaches every term.
The square was added, not subtracted.

optionNotes.option: The quadratic with its first term's sign changed
optionNotes.why: The minus must reach every term, and only a bracket carries it that far.

optionNotes.option: The two expressions side by side and collect straight away
optionNotes.why: Collecting straight away is where the signs of the later terms get lost.

noteBlocks.md:
Expand any pair, then multiply the quadratic by the third bracket.
Count six products, then collect in descending powers.
Write both ends first: the x terms multiplied, the numbers multiplied.
Keep a reversed bracket as printed, and bracket anything you subtract.

Usually 3 marks, as a part of its own (Summer 2019 Q12(i), Summer 2026 Q5) or as the first step of a longer question (Summer 2022 Q9(a), Summer 2023 Q12(iii)): one mark for a pair expanded, one for the six products, one for the collected cubic. Stuck: write any pair out; the answer is the same whichever you start with.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

steps.decision: Keep (2 − 3x) as printed: 2x + 8 − 3x² − 12x, collected.

options: Turning the bracket round would change the expression and every sign of the answer
The first two brackets must always be expanded first
A bracket with the number first cannot be multiplied
whyMenu.explain: $(2 - 3x)$ and $(3x - 2)$ differ by a factor of $-1$, so swapping them flips every sign. Any pair may go first; this one is simply convenient.

steps.decision: The x of the last bracket meets all three terms.
The −1 meets all three too: six products, and every sign flips.
Collect in descending powers. The ends check: −3x³ and 2 × 4 × (−1) = −8.

options: The x³ term is the three x terms multiplied and the constant the three numbers multiplied
A cubic always ends in a negative number
whyMenu.explain: $(-3x)(x)(x) = -3x^{3}$ and $2 \times 4 \times (-1) = -8$: both ends agree with the answer, so no product at either end is missing.

items.stem: What is the first move when you expand $(x+1)(x+2)(x+5)$?

options.text: Multiply two of the brackets together, then multiply that quadratic by the bracket that is left
options.feedback: That is the route the scheme is written around, and it keeps every product visible.

options.text: Multiply the three $x$ terms together and the three numbers together
options.feedback: That gives only the two end terms, $x^{3}$ and $10$. The middle of the cubic is missing, so the answer is short by two terms.

options.text: Add the three brackets and then multiply the result by $x$
options.feedback: Brackets written next to each other are multiplied, never added. Adding them changes the expression completely.

items.stem: A quadratic with three terms is multiplied by a bracket with two terms. How many products are there before you collect like terms?
items.skill: Count the products so none is dropped

options.feedback: Three terms times two terms is six products. Counting them is the quickest way to catch a missing one.
Five means one product was never written. Every term of the quadratic has to meet both terms of the bracket.
Three is what you get when the quadratic is multiplied by one term of the bracket only. The other term still has to be used.

items.stem: In the expansion of $(2x+3)(4x-1)(x+2)$, what is the coefficient of $x^{3}$?
items.skill: Read the cubic coefficient as the product of the three x coefficients

options.feedback: The $x^{3}$ term can only come from the three $x$ terms multiplied together: $2 \times 4 \times 1$.
The coefficients are multiplied, not added. Adding them would be right for collecting like terms, not for forming the highest power.
That is the product of the three constants, which gives the constant term of the expansion rather than the coefficient of $x^{3}$.

items.stem: In the expansion of $(x-3)(2x+5)(x-1)$, what is the constant term?
items.skill: Read the constant term as the product of the three constants

options.feedback: The constant comes from the three numbers only: $(-3) \times 5 \times (-1)$. Two negatives make it positive.
The size is right and the sign is not. Count the negative brackets: an even number of them leaves the constant positive.
The three constants are multiplied. Adding them is what happens to like terms later, in the middle of the expansion.

items.stem: Not yet taught here: a warm-up from earlier maths. What is $(x + 3)(x - 5)$ multiplied out?

options.feedback: $x^{2} - 5x + 3x - 15$, collected.
The two middle products, −5x and +3x, are missing.
The middle products are −5x and +3x, which make −2x, not 8x.

items.stem: Not yet taught here: a warm-up from earlier maths. What is $-(x^{2} - 4x + 2)$ without the bracket?
items.skill: A minus in front of a bracket

options.feedback: The minus changes the sign of every term.
Only the first sign changed; the minus reaches every term.
The minus in front was dropped altogether.

items.stem: Not yet taught here: a warm-up from earlier maths. What is $3x^{2} - 5x + 2x^{2} + 7x$ collected?

options.feedback: The x² terms make 5x² and the x terms make 2x.
Unlike terms do not combine, and powers are not added when terms are.
−5x + 7x is +2x.
$(x + 6)(x - 1) = x^{2} + 5x - 6$, then its three terms meet the $x$ and the $-2$: six products, collected.
Only the x of the last bracket was used; the −2 must meet all three terms.
Only the two ends were kept; the middle products are missing.

scheme.for: two brackets expanded correctly, e.g. x² + 3x + 2
multiplied by the third bracket and collected: x³ + 8x² + 17x + 10

hints: Multiply two of the brackets first; any pair will do.
The first pair gives $x^{2}+3x+2$.
Three terms times two terms is six products, then collect.
parts.workedSolution:
$(x+1)(x+2) = x^{2}+3x+2$, so the expression is $(x^{2}+3x+2)(x+5)$.
Multiplying every term by $x$ gives $x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x$ and multiplying every term by $5$ gives $5x^{2}+15x+10$.
Collecting like terms: $x^{3}+8x^{2}+17x+10$.

commonErrors.feedback: The method-and-working mark is for multiplying the quadratic by the whole of (x+5), and only the $x$ was used. Go back and multiply each of the three terms by 5 as well, then collect.

Every product is right, so the method-and-working mark for the first pair is safe. The last mark is for the collected form in descending powers, so gather the like terms and write one term for each power.

parts.stem:
A storage box is a cuboid with edges of length $(x+1)$ cm, $(x+4)$ cm and $(2x-3)$ cm.
Expand and simplify the expression for its volume
$(x+1)(x+4)(2x-3)$

scheme.for: two brackets expanded correctly, e.g. x² + 5x + 4
accept: any pair of the three brackets

scheme.for: that quadratic multiplied by the remaining bracket, giving the six products 2x³ + 10x² + 8x and -3x² - 15x - 12
like terms collected: 2x³ + 7x² - 7x - 12

hints: Start with the two brackets that have a single $x$.
Multiply all three terms by $2x$, then all three by $-3$.

commonErrors.feedback: The method-and-working mark is for multiplying the quadratic by the whole of (2x-3), and only the $2x$ was used. Go back and multiply each of the three terms by -3 as well, then collect.

Every product is right, so the method-and-working marks for the two multiplications are safe. The last mark is for the collected form in descending powers, so gather the like terms and write one term for each power.

parts.stem: Calculate the volume of the box when $x = 5$.

scheme.for: substituting x = 5 into either the three brackets or the expanded cubic, e.g. 6 × 9 × 7

ignore: a missing unit on the answer line

hints: The three edges become 6 cm, 9 cm and 7 cm.
Either multiply the three edges or substitute into your answer to part (a); both should give the same number.
parts.workedSolution:
The edges are $6$ cm, $9$ cm and $7$ cm, so the volume is $6 \times 9 \times 7 = 378$ cm³.
Substituting $x = 5$ into $2x^{3}+7x^{2}-7x-12$ gives the same value, which is the check worth making.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the value of the expansion with only the $2x$ used from the last bracket. Substituting into the three brackets directly, 6 × 9 × 7, is the safer route and it also checks part (a).
That comes from an expansion built out of the first terms and the last terms only. The volume is the product of the three edge lengths, 6 × 9 × 7.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to expand and simplify $(x-3)(2x+1)(x+4)$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The 4 in the second bracket was multiplied by the 2x² only. It has to multiply all three terms of 2x² - 5x - 3, which gives 8x² - 20x - 12.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first method-and-working mark is safe: (x - 3)(2x + 1) is expanded correctly. The second mark is for multiplying the quadratic by the whole of the third bracket, and three products are missing, so it is lost. Count the products before you collect: three terms times two terms is six. Examiners in Summer 2023 traced most of the errors in this kind of expansion to terms left out when brackets were not used.

prompts.prompt: How do you expand three brackets?
prompts.answer: Expand any two, then multiply that quadratic by the third bracket.

prompts.prompt: How many products does a quadratic times a bracket give?
prompts.answer: Six: three terms times two terms, before collecting.

prompts.prompt: What gives the x³ term and the constant of three brackets?
prompts.answer: The x terms multiplied together, and the numbers multiplied together.

prompts.prompt: Why bracket an expansion you are subtracting?
prompts.answer: So the minus changes the sign of every term inside it.
